title: How to read an RC passage
summary: Read for the main point and the author's view, give each paragraph a job, track who believes what, and keep highlighting light.

slides.title: Read to understand, not to memorize
body: Reading Comprehension rewards knowing what the passage is doing, not remembering its details. Details you can look up; the structure you can’t, unless you built it while reading.
Every passage is either mainly informing you about something or mainly persuading you of something. Decide which in the first paragraph or two, and you know what to listen for.
Most questions come down to one test: is this answer supported by the text? Treat them like must-be-true questions about the passage.
slides.callout: By the end of the passage you should be able to say the main point in one sentence.

steps.label: First lines: topic and style
steps.do: What is this about, and is the author reporting or arguing? Look for an established view that is about to be challenged.

steps.label: One job per paragraph
steps.do: After each paragraph, give it a short label: introduces the debate, gives the critics’ view, offers evidence, answers an objection.

steps.label: Track the voices
steps.do: Note who holds each view: the author, critics, some historians, the traditional account. Questions often ask which view belongs to whom.

steps.label: Mark the pivots
steps.do: However, but, yet and nevertheless are where the passage turns. The author’s own view usually follows a pivot.

steps.label: Catch the author’s tone
steps.do: Words like persuasive, overstated, promising and unfortunately reveal the author’s attitude. Note them.

steps.label: Say the main point
steps.do: Before the questions, state the main point in one sentence: not just the topic, not every detail.

slides.title: Five passage shapes and what to track
head: Shape
What it does
Track
rows: Sets out a view, then challenges it.
Each side’s claim and where the author lands.
The thesis and the support in each paragraph.
Describes something puzzling and offers explanations.
Each explanation and which one the author favors.
Describes a problem and weighs responses.
The problem, each proposed fix and its limits.
Profiles a person, work or movement.
What makes the subject significant and any reassessment.

traps.name: Detail hoarding
traps.tell: Trying to remember every name and date. Note where details are, not what they are.

traps.name: Missing the turn
traps.tell: Taking the first view described as the author’s. The author often introduces a view only to reject it.

traps.name: Topic, not point
traps.tell: A main point that only names the subject. Ask what the author is saying about the subject.

traps.name: Outside knowledge
traps.tell: Answering from what you know about the topic. The passage is the only source.

traps.name: Heavy highlighting
traps.tell: Highlighting whole sentences turns the passage yellow. Mark pivots, viewpoints and the author’s tone words only.

slides.title: Cheat card
lines: Mark pivots and tone words; skip the details.
Say the main point in one sentence before the questions.
Every answer must be supported by the text.
